---
title: "5 · Designs & Clifford Ensembles"
---

A Haar-random unitary on $N$ qubits needs exponentially many real parameters to
specify and cannot be sampled or stored efficiently. Most calculations, however,
touch the Haar measure only through its low moments, the averages of
$U^{\otimes t} \otimes \bar U^{\otimes t}$. A unitary $t$-design is a finite
ensemble that reproduces those averages up to order $t$, which is all the
randomness the second-moment and fourth-moment formulas of Parts 3 and 6
actually consume.

The Clifford group is the standard construction. It is an exact $3$-design and,
by the Gottesman-Knill theorem, can be sampled and simulated classically in
polynomial time. That same simulability marks what a design leaves out. Clifford
circuits reach near-maximal entanglement, yet their out-of-time-ordered
correlator takes only the values $0$ and $4$, with no smooth Lyapunov growth, so
entanglement and genuine scrambling come apart here.

The missing resource is nonstabilizerness, or magic, the degree to which a state
lies outside the set reachable by Clifford operations on computational basis
states. The stabilizer Rényi entropy quantifies it from the expansion of the
state over Pauli operators, vanishing exactly on stabilizer states and positive
otherwise, and it is the quantity that separates a $3$-design from full Haar
randomness.

- [Stabilizer Rényi entropy](../notebooks/ch5/solution_ch5_stabilizer_renyi_entropy.ipynb), measuring "magic," the resource beyond entanglement.
